goal.description: Find out what is true and answer every stakeholder honestly: engage the CBC investigation on the record, run a genuine investigation into the substance of the allegations - not the source of the leak - protect members from any risk that turns out to be real, satisfy the regulator and the board with facts and process, and bring public trust and regulator confidence back above healthy thresholds.
goal.win_conditions_note: Advisory only. The exercise is won by resolving the STORY (the final beat reached, or the attack chain fully contained), NOT by these numeric thresholds. They colour how costly the win reads; they never gate it.
goal.ending: Crisis resolved: the substance of the allegations is established and owned, any real member risk is remediated, the investigation and its process withstand scrutiny, and the board, regulator, staff, and members are confident in the outcome. The exercise concludes.

intro.narrative: CBC's investigative unit has a package, and this morning they sent you the questions. Someone inside {{org_name}} - a respected, long-tenured employee with legitimate access - has handed them internal risk reports, email chains, and committee memos. The package alleges that {{org_name}} is knowingly exposing members to risk: warnings about lending practices were repeated in report after report, executives 'noted' them and moved on, and the internal numbers show the concerns were significant and growing. Here is the problem: nobody - including the executive team - knows yet how much of it is true. Some documents are real. Some claims read like honest concern stretched into damning narrative. CBC is working sources and has a deadline. Inside {{org_name}}, staff are already speculating about who talked. The regulator has started calling. The board wants answers. You are the executive team, holding a crisis you cannot yet verify - and every audience is asking at once.
intro.company_info: {{org_name}} is a mid-sized, member-owned credit union. As a cooperative, its core promise is that members come before growth - which is exactly the promise the whistleblower's package calls a lie. The regulator expects issues to be self-reported, distinguishes sharply between organizations that come forward and organizations that get exposed, and treats whistleblower treatment as a governance signal in itself. A leak from a trusted insider is not a security failure; it is a trust failure, and everyone inside knows it.

learning_objectives: Practice answering an unseen-cards crisis: responding honestly before you know what is true
Choose between investigating the substance and hunting the source - and feel the cost of the wrong choice
Engage an investigative reporter without spinning, stonewalling, or lying
Manage simultaneous pressure from media, regulator, board, and staff
Self-report credibly to a regulator and defend governance process under scrutiny

attack_chain.name: How it got out
attack_chain.symptom: The package was assembled by someone trusted with legitimate access: quarterly risk reports, an email chain in which a director says a concentration concern 'fits within the board's risk appetite for now,' and a memo about member complaints. There was no hack and no betrayal of a firewall - the vulnerability is that the documents were real, kept somewhere an insider could hold them, and damning enough in combination that someone chose to leave with them. Until the team establishes what the leaker actually had access to, the source narrows to a handful of serious people.

attack_chain.name: How it spread
attack_chain.symptom: The story's escalation engine is stakeholders with the same questions: CBC is working sources inside and out, other outlets are calling for confirmation, staff are speculating in internal channels after a screenshot of the reporter's email circulated, and the regulator has been contacted as part of CBC's standard verification. Fragments are leaking ahead of the broadcast - a subreddit thread has two of the documents - and the board learned about it from a director's spouse before the executive team could brief them.

attack_chain.name: What it's costing
attack_chain.symptom: The bill is coming due before the facts are clear: CBC's story is nearly ready and the team still cannot say what is true; the regulator's questions have the shape of a file being opened; the board is demanding a written account of what leadership knew; staff are asking whether {{org_name}} is hiding something - and whether speaking up internally is now dangerous; and if the story publishes with the organization still unable to answer, the takeaway is not 'the allegations were unproven' but '{{org_name}} couldn't say.'

beats.name: Step 1 — Answer four audiences before you know the truth
beats.narrative: CBC has a deadline, staff are speculating, the regulator is circling, and the board wants a written account - and the team does not yet know how much of the package is true. Step 1 is to set the posture: engage honestly on the record with the reporter, brief the board before they read about it, give staff something true to hold, and resist the temptation to hunt the source. Posture decisions made now decide whether everything that follows is read as good faith or cover-up.

developments.text: CBC publishes a first story before the team is ready, quoting the documents and naming the drift in the concentration number - the group is now responding to a published fact, not a request for comment.

beats.name: Step 2 — Establish what is actually true
beats.narrative: The posture is set. Now the harder work: run a genuine investigation into the substance - the risk reports, the email chain, the concentration number that drifted for four quarters, the decisions that were consciously accepted and the ones that quietly slipped - while answering the regulator's questions and defending the board's risk-appetite decisions without hiding behind them. If Step 1 was honest, the investigation gets the benefit of the doubt; if it was defensive, every finding leaks before it can be released.

developments.text: The investigation finds the whistleblower kept a second set of files the journalists have not seen, and someone inside is quietly trying to identify the source - the group must protect the source while the truth keeps growing.

beats.name: Step 3 — Remediate the real risk
beats.narrative: The facts are established. Step 3 is to eradicate the real risk the reports exposed: fix the concentration exposure the numbers confirmed, remediate any genuine member harm and make those members whole, correct what the documents show was exaggerated, and protect the source while doing it. Show the group that acting on uncomfortable truths is a separate job from managing the disclosure.

developments.text: The remediation exposes an uncomfortable truth: the concentration risk is larger than the reports claimed, so fixing it means an expensive exposure reduction the board never budgeted for - acting honestly now has a real cost.

beats.name: Step 4 — Prove the culture changed
beats.narrative: The risk is being remediated. The final step is recovery: prove to staff, members, and the regulator that raising concerns now leads somewhere, restore the confidence the crisis shook, publish what changed, and close out on an honest account of what was missed and fixed. The story should end on whether the organization is one that can hear bad news — at a cost, but earned.

developments.text: Staff who once raised concerns ask the group to prove, not promise, that speaking up is now safe - and the regulator asks for evidence that the culture change is real, not a statement of intent.

dm_brief.situation: An anonymous but credible whistleblower - a respected long-tenured insider with legitimate access - has sent CBC's investigative unit a package of internal risk reports, emails, and memos alleging that {{org_name}} knowingly exposes members to lending risk and that executives ignored repeated, documented warnings. The uncomfortable truth: the executive team does not yet know how much is true. The risk reports are real; some warnings were genuinely discussed and genuinely judged manageable; some of the framing in the package is an unfair stretch; some of it may be worse than anyone has admitted yet. CBC has questions and a deadline, staff are speculating about who leaked, an innocent colleague is being quietly blamed, the regulator has started calling, and the board demands answers. The team must decide what posture to take - substance or spin, investigation or inquisition - while every audience demands an answer the team does not yet have.
dm_brief.stakes: If handled poorly: the story becomes the cover-up, not the allegations; the leaker-hunt leaks and reads as retaliation; the regulator concludes {{org_name}} hides things; the board loses confidence in leadership; staff conclude that raising concerns internally is career-ending - and the next problem goes straight to the press without the courtesy of a package first. If handled well: the substance is established honestly, real member risk is fixed, the process withstands scrutiny, and even the whistleblower's worst framing meets a response people can respect.

key_actors.name: The CBC investigative reporter
key_actors.interests: A rigorous story that holds: verifying every document, hearing {{org_name}}'s side, publishing regardless of whether {{org_name}} engages.
key_actors.knowledge: Has the package, has confirmed several documents independently, and has already contacted the regulator for comment as part of verification. Her deadline is days, not weeks - and she has seen organizations stonewall before.

key_actors.name: The whistleblower
key_actors.interests: To be proven right, and to see the risk to members fixed - not money, not revenge.
key_actors.knowledge: Knows the reports are real because they wrote or received several of them; claims to have tried internal channels first and been 'managed.' Their identity is unknown, but the access pattern narrows it to a handful of serious people - and colleagues are already guessing.

key_actors.name: The Chief Risk Officer
key_actors.interests: Wants the actual risk picture established honestly - quietly if possible.
key_actors.knowledge: The truth is complicated: the warnings in the reports were real and were discussed at risk committee; some were acted on, some were consciously accepted within appetite, and one - the concentration number - has been drifting upward for four quarters while the plan to fix it kept slipping.

key_actors.name: The regulator's case lead
key_actors.interests: Whether {{org_name}} self-reports, whether members are at risk, and whether governance actually works here.
key_actors.knowledge: Has been contacted by CBC as part of verification and has seen enough packages in a career to know that 'the org investigates the messenger' is the first sign of rot. Distinguishes sharply between organizations that come forward and organizations that get caught.

key_actors.name: The Board chair
key_actors.interests: The board's own exposure - several memos went to committee - and not being blindsided again.
key_actors.knowledge: Learned of the story from another director before the executive team's briefing landed; wants a written account of what leadership knew, when, and why the risk appetite decisions were made - and is quietly worried the answer is 'by us, reluctantly.'

key_actors.name: The internal communications lead
key_actors.interests: Needs to tell staff something true - today.
key_actors.knowledge: Staff channels are on fire: speculation about the leaker, worry about retaliation, and a growing sense that leadership cares more about the leak than the risk. Whatever she sends will be screenshotted within the hour.

pressure_points: CBC moves the deadline up and sends a pointed follow-up: 'We have a recording of an internal meeting where the concentration risk was described as "embarrassing if it ever got out." Comment?'
A screenshot of the reporter's original email circulates internally with the comment 'who talked?' - and a colleague from risk is quietly blamed by name.
The regulator calls: they are aware of the pending coverage and want to know whether {{org_name}} intends to self-report - or wait.
The board chair calls an emergency session and asks for a written account of what leadership knew - before CBC provides its own version.
A second package arrives - this one to a different outlet, with more recent quarters and a chart the team has never seen before.
rules_of_play: Never propose actions, present a menu of choices, or suggest what the group should do. Only react to what the group decides.

Keep the story advancing by injecting NEW DEVELOPMENTS (a reporter pushes harder, new information surfaces, a deadline lands, a complication emerges), not by telling the team what to decide or do. Never write 'the team needs to...', 'consider...', or 'the next step is to...'.
A single turn can contain 2-3 coordinated actions across departments (e.g. comms statement + fraud freeze + regulator update). Address each in your response.
Keep the tone realistic for a credit union: members matter, trust is the product, regulation is real.
Show consequences of the roll, but let the group's stated actions drive the logic.
Update the tracked metrics (budget, public_trust, regulator_confidence, security_posture, containment, eradication, recovery) to reflect outcomes.
Reveal an attack-chain stage when the group's investigation plausibly uncovers it; mark it contained when the group neutralizes it.
If the group stalls with no clear action for a while, inject a pressure point to move things.
Detection and response are limited resources: the group cannot do everything at once, and activating monitoring costs budget.

Keep the session winnable: a good action on a good roll should stabilize or improve metrics, not punish them. Reserve large negative deltas for genuinely bad outcomes. Do not make it a foregone loss by turn 4-5.

The situation can collapse into a narrated LOSS: if public_trust AND regulator_confidence both fall to 20 or below for consecutive turns, the story ends badly - members lose faith, the regulator escalates, the board loses confidence in the response. Narrate that strain realistically as confidence falls, but reward competent, coordinated response with recovery.

The complete response arc is contain, then eradicate, then recover. Reward eradication and recovery efforts when the group attempts them; a group that only does PR and containment keeps struggling - the story keeps biting, the regulator stays unsatisfied - until it closes out the full arc.

events.text: CBC's investigation unit sends a pointed follow-up with a deadline attached: they have verified several documents independently and are preparing to run the story with '{{org_name}} did not respond to repeated requests for comment.'

Internal speculation explodes: a screenshot of the reporter's email circulates in staff channels with 'who talked?' - and a well-liked colleague from the risk team is quietly blamed by name. Staff morale sours and the word 'retaliation' starts appearing in print.

The regulator calls: they are aware of the pending CBC coverage, have been contacted during verification, and want to know whether {{org_name}} intends to self-report the issues - or wait to be told about them.

The board chair calls an emergency session and demands a written account of what leadership knew and when - noting that CBC appears to be assembling one already, and that several memos in the package went to the board's own committees.

CBC publishes part one: 'Members at risk, warnings ignored: documents from inside {{org_name}}.' The piece is measured but damning - real documents, a timeline of repeated warnings, and a line about 'repeated requests for comment.' Within hours, other outlets are aggregating it and members are asking what is true.

1.twist: Your first response is a disaster: the organization chooses the inquisition. IT access logs get pulled, a suspected leaker is suspended, and CBC runs the suspension as proof of retaliation. Trust collapses.

2.twist: The response backfires: a combative legal threat to CBC is reported as an attack on the press, and the regulator's interest hardens into a formal case.

3.twist: Scrambling to find the source turns into a witch-hunt that leaks, and the staff speculation poisons trust internally exactly when the organization needs solidarity.

4.twist: The response reads as defensive and legalistic; the regulator's case lead notes the organization is 'managing perception rather than the risk'.

5.twist: Your response is procedural and bloodless, and it reads as a brush-off; the whistleblower's advocates say the organization 'still doesn't get it'.

6.twist: Partial: the organization engages CBC and avoids making it worse, but the substance stays unaddressed and the documents do the talking.

7.twist: Mixed: you pledge transparency, but a leaked internal email shows a board member dismissing the concern - the pledge and the leak land the same day, and neither is fully believed.

8.twist: Modest gain: an honest internal review begins and the regulator accepts the cooperative gesture, though CBC's deadline forces something out.

9.twist: A quiet win: you get ahead of a document request and hand the regulator a clean, complete record, which buys credibility for the harder questions ahead.

10.twist: Solid win: the organization establishes the real risk picture honestly - some warnings were valid, one number has drifted up - and acts on it.

11.twist: A lucky break: the regulator, having seen your proactive disclosure, publicly describes the organization as cooperative rather than evasive - the frame shifts in your favour.

12.twist: Strong handling: the organization protects the whistleblower's anonymity, engages the facts, and commits to fixing what the reports exposed.

13.twist: The group's handling reframes the story: the legitimate concerns are owned, the framing exaggerations are gently corrected with evidence, and trust steadies.

14.twist: A respected former regulator agrees to review your governance process, lending the response independent weight.

15.twist: Strong play: an independent review confirms both the real warnings and the spin, and the organization's handling earns quiet credibility.

16.twist: Real control: the story becomes about how the organization responded to uncomfortable truths, and the regulator closes its posture to monitored cooperation.

17.twist: Strong play: you voluntarily disclose a real if minor governance failure the whistleblower didn't even raise, which badly undercuts the 'what else are they hiding' narrative.

18.twist: Near-decisive: full transparency with the regulator, real remediation, and protection for the source - the story loses its angle entirely.

19.twist: A commanding turn: the warnings are validated, the fix is real and visible, and the whistleblower's core point is publicly answered.

20.twist: A clean, devastatingly effective response: the team commits to substance over spin - it engages CBC on the record, protects the whistleblower, fixes the concentration risk, and publishes the remediation. Both the regulator and the outlet call it exemplary.

end_conditions.ending: The collapse: CBC's part two lands and nothing meets it - no facts, no accountability, no leader in front of the story. Members read the documents and draw their own conclusions, the regulator arrives with a self-reporting mandate instead of questions, and the board's emergency session ends in resignations. {{org_name}} stops being an organization that answers for itself. The exercise concludes as a loss.
Time ran out on the scheduled exercise.
